title: State-selective dynamical freezing in driven Rydberg atom chains
summary: Dynamical freezing, the near-complete suppression of dynamics at special drive frequencies, offers a route to mitigating Floquet heating in periodically driven quantum systems. In interacting systems, however, the energy cost of each transition depends on the many-body configuration, so that the freezing condition itself becomes state dependent. We study this dependence in periodically driven Rydberg atom chains under single- and bi-frequency driving. Using Floquet perturbation theory, we show that each spin flip is characterised by a single interference amplitude set by its local interaction shift, and that a state freezes only where the amplitudes of all its available flips vanish simultaneously. This picture accounts quantitatively for the shift and proliferation of freezing frequencies with interatomic spacing and for the response of entire families of initial states, which are sorted by a single local motif. Freezing is strong only within a window of spacings bounded by interaction tails on one side and nearest-neighbour excitation facilitation on the other, outside of which the advantage of bi-frequency driving is lost. In the regime of large detuning amplitude, where freezing points are numerous and the perturbative description is controlled, this window leaves almost no room for the PXP limit.

AI.tldr: Dynamical freezing in driven Rydberg chains is shown to be state dependent: each spin flip carries a single interference amplitude set by its local interaction shift, and a state freezes only when all its available flips have vanishing amplitude simultaneously, which quantitatively explains how freezing frequencies shift, proliferate, and respond across state families.
AI.motivation: Floquet heating limits periodically driven quantum systems. Dynamical freezing—near-total suppression of dynamics at special drive frequencies—can mitigate this, but in interacting systems the energy cost of each transition is configuration dependent, so the freezing condition itself becomes state dependent. This work aims to characterize that dependence.
AI.method: Floquet perturbation theory applied to periodically driven Rydberg atom chains under single- and bi-frequency driving. Each spin flip is assigned a single interference amplitude governed by its local interaction shift; freezing of a state requires simultaneous vanishing of amplitudes for all its available flips. The theory is compared against the behavior of entire families of initial states, classified by a single local motif.
AI.result: The local-amplitude picture quantitatively accounts for the shift and proliferation of freezing frequencies with interatomic spacing, and for the response of whole state families sorted by a single local motif. Freezing is strong only within a finite window of spacings, bounded on one side by interaction tails and on the other by nearest-neighbour excitation facilitation; outside this window the advantage of bi-frequency driving disappears. In the large-detuning-amplitude regime, where freezing points are numerous and the perturbative description is controlled, this window leaves almost no room for the PXP limit.
AI.conclusion: State-dependent freezing in interacting driven systems is governed by local interference amplitudes, yielding a predictive, motif-based classification of which states freeze and where. The viable parameter window for strong freezing is narrow and constrained by interaction tails and facilitation, and in the controlled large-detuning regime it is largely incompatible with the PXP description.

title: Mitigating large circuits with a learned small-circuit mitigator
comment: 41 pages, 25 figures, 9 tables, comments are welcome
summary: Learning-based quantum error mitigation infers noise-free results from noisy measurement data. However, exact training labels become prohibitively expensive to compute as circuits grow, and the generalization capability of a trained model to infer accurate results on circuits of depths and sizes it was not trained on poses a challenge. We show that circuit cutting allows such a model to be reused on circuits larger than those it was trained on. We benchmark this approach against zero-noise extrapolation, Clifford data regression, and probabilistic error cancellation on simulated circuits several times wider and deeper than the training circuits. On random-circuit chains, the fragment-wise mitigator removes most of the reconstructed error. For a holographic Ising-chain eigensolver under a fixed shot budget, it recovers most of the noise-induced energy error, close to 90\% or more, and outperforms Clifford data regression and probabilistic error cancellation. Since the mitigator is trained once and needs no additional circuits or noise amplification at inference, its cost is paid up front rather than for every new circuit. The approach is also modular. Any improvement to the small-circuit mitigator, such as retraining on larger fragments or on device-specific noise, carries over directly to every circuit that can be cut into such fragments. Our proposal thus offers a practical route to bringing learned error mitigation to quantum computations far beyond the reach of exact training labels, provided they can be partitioned with a moderate number of cuts.

AI.tldr: A learned error mitigator trained on small circuits is combined with circuit cutting so the same model can be reused on much wider/deeper circuits than it was trained on, recovering up to ~90% of noise-induced energy error.
AI.motivation: Learning-based quantum error mitigation requires exact noise-free training labels, which become prohibitively expensive as circuits grow. Moreover, a trained model's generalization to circuits of unseen depth and size is questionable. The authors seek a way to reuse a small-circuit mitigator on larger circuits without needing exact labels for those larger circuits.
AI.method: The approach uses circuit cutting to partition large circuits into fragments matching the size of training circuits. A fragment-wise learned mitigator, trained once on small fragments, is applied to each fragment, and results are reconstructed from the cut circuits. The method is benchmarked on simulated circuits several times wider and deeper than the training circuits against zero-noise extrapolation, Clifford data regression, and probabilistic error cancellation.
AI.result: On random-circuit chains, the fragment-wise mitigator removes most of the reconstructed error. For a holographic Ising-chain eigensolver under a fixed shot budget, it recovers most of the noise-induced energy error (close to 90% or more) and outperforms Clifford data regression and probabilistic error cancellation.
AI.conclusion: Circuit cutting enables a single, up-front-trained mitigator to be reused on circuits far beyond the reach of exact training labels, with no extra circuits or noise amplification at inference. The approach is modular: improvements to the small-circuit mitigator (e.g., retraining on larger fragments or device-specific noise) carry over directly to any circuit cut into such fragments, offering a practical route to scaling learned error mitigation to larger quantum computations given a moderate number of cuts.

title: Comment on phase vortex lattices in neutron interferometry
summary: We present a phase-based theoretical description of the four-plate crystal neutron interferometer (LLLL geometry) originally introduced by Heinrich et al. [Z. Phys. B 72, 357 (1988)]. The LLLL interferometer can be interpreted as two coupled LLL interferometric loops that share partial beam paths, leading to characteristic interference phenomena beyond the standard three-plate configuration. Using a coherent beam-splitting model we derive the forward intensity in terms of loop phase sums and recover the cosine-sum structure reported in Refs.[1,2]. Based on these results we analyze the phase dependence of the forward beam in the presence of localized phase objects, such as wedges inserted into individual partial beams. In experiments presented in [2], the LLLL interferometer is used to generate a periodic array of intensity in two dimensions by which the authors claim to demonstrate a phase vortex grating of significant extrinsic orbital angular momentum (OAM). However, the same interference patterns are predicted by simulating a coherent superposition of {beam paths} along different interferometer loops and experiencing phase shifts in each loop due to two wedges that are perpendicular to each other, without assuming any neutron OAM.

AI.tldr: A phase-based model of the four-plate LLLL neutron interferometer reproduces the reported cosine-sum interference patterns and the two-dimensional intensity arrays using only loop phase sums from two perpendicular wedges, without invoking neutron orbital angular momentum.
AI.motivation: The four-plate LLLL interferometer has been claimed to demonstrate a phase vortex grating carrying significant extrinsic OAM. The authors seek a conventional phase-based description to test whether OAM is actually required to explain the observed interference.
AI.method: Treating the LLLL geometry as two coupled LLL loops sharing partial beam paths, the authors apply a coherent beam-splitting model to derive the forward-beam intensity in terms of loop phase sums, then simulate localized phase objects (two mutually perpendicular wedges) in individual partial beams.
AI.result: The model recovers the cosine-sum structure reported previously and predicts the same periodic two-dimensional intensity arrays that were attributed to an OAM phase vortex grating, purely from coherent superposition of beam paths with loop-dependent phase shifts.
AI.conclusion: The observed LLLL interference patterns do not require neutron OAM; a standard phase-sum description accounts for them, so the OAM interpretation of the earlier experiment is not supported by these results.

title: Corrections to the IPR in the localized phase of the Anderson model on the Bethe lattice
comment: 10 pages, 4 figures (including End Matter). Companion to the longer paper "Anomalous corrections to the inverse participation ratio in the localized phase on the Bethe lattice: insights from a solvable 'toy' non-linear sigma-model"
summary: We show that finite-size effects in the localized phase of the Anderson model on the Bethe lattice are highly anomalous. On random regular graphs of $N$ sites the inverse participation ratio (IPR) approaches its thermodynamic-limit value as $I_2(N)-I_2^\infty\sim N^{-κ(W)}$, with a disorder-dependent exponent $0<κ<1$ throughout the localized phase, and the same exponent governs the correction due to a finite imaginary regulator, $I_2(η)-I_2^\infty\simη^{κ(W)}$. We derive $κ= 2β-1$, with $β$ the power-law tail exponent of the local density of states distribution, in a solvable model sharing the criticality of the Anderson model on the Bethe lattice. We then show that the same mechanism operates in the Anderson model itself, and find quantitative agreement with the numerics. A self-consistent one-loop treatment of the loops of finite graphs independently reproduces the finite-size corrections. Physically, a spectral identity and an exact sum rule tie both corrections to rare Mott-like resonances hybridizing distant localized eigenstates: a finite graph lacks the resonant pairs whose centers would lie farther apart than its size allows. Our results identify the scaling variable needed to extrapolate IPR data to the thermodynamic limit.

AI.tldr: Finite-size and finite-regulator corrections to the IPR in the localized phase of the Anderson model on the Bethe lattice scale as a disorder-dependent power law, with exponent κ = 2β − 1 tied to rare Mott-like resonances between distant localized states.
AI.motivation: Extrapolating localization observables such as the inverse participation ratio (IPR) to the thermodynamic limit requires knowing how they approach it. On the Bethe lattice / random regular graphs the localized phase is expected to be well understood, yet the finite-size (and finite-imaginary-regulator) approach was assumed conventional. The authors aim to characterize the actual finite-size scaling of the IPR in the localized phase and identify the physical origin of the corrections and the correct scaling variable.
AI.method: Analytical derivation of the IPR finite-size correction exponent in a solvable model that shares the criticality of the Anderson model on the Bethe lattice, mapping κ to the power-law tail exponent β of the local density of states distribution (κ = 2β − 1). Comparison with direct numerics on random regular graphs. A self-consistent one-loop treatment of loops on finite graphs to independently reproduce the corrections. Physical interpretation via a spectral identity and an exact sum rule linking corrections to rare Mott-like resonances that hybridize distant localized eigenstates.
AI.result: The IPR approaches its thermodynamic-limit value as I2(N) − I2∞ ∼ N^(−κ(W)) with 0 < κ < 1 throughout the localized phase, disorder-dependent; the same exponent controls the finite-imaginary-regulator correction I2(η) − I2∞ ∼ η^(κ(W)). κ = 2β − 1, with β the tail exponent of the local density of states distribution. The same mechanism operates in the Anderson model itself, in quantitative agreement with numerics; the one-loop loop treatment independently reproduces the finite-size corrections.
AI.conclusion: Finite-size effects in the localized phase on the Bethe lattice are anomalous, governed by rare Mott-like resonances between distant localized eigenstates, which a finite graph cannot host beyond its size. The results yield the scaling variable needed to extrapolate IPR data to the thermodynamic limit and identify resonant-pair statistics as the controlling physics.

title: Distant Bell States via Measured Spin Chain Dynamics
summary: Preparing distant qubits in Bell states is a core requirement for quantum networking and distributed quantum computation. The nonequilibrium unitary dynamics of spin chains have been envisaged as a convenient quantum channel for intra-chip communications. Typically it establishes mixed entangled states between its remote ends, to be purified by entanglement distillation after several uses of the channel to obtain Bell states. Here we show how the establishment of entanglement via spin chain dynamics can be (a) sped up and (b) made to yield a pure entangled state after a single usage of the channel, which is upgradable to a Bell-state without the complexity of purification. To this end, we intersperse unitary evolution for some period with measurements on intermediary spins. We explore two different measurements: a measurement that post-selects for a ground state; and local measurements in the computational basis. We illustrate the mechanism with qubits coupled to the ends of a 1D $XY$ spin chain.

AI.tldr: Interspersing unitary spin-chain evolution with measurements on intermediary spins speeds up entanglement generation between distant qubits and yields a pure entangled state in a single channel use, upgradable to a Bell state without distillation.
AI.motivation: Spin chains are attractive quantum channels for intra-chip communication, but their nonequilibrium unitary dynamics typically produce mixed entangled states at the remote ends, requiring repeated channel uses and entanglement distillation to obtain Bell states. The authors aim to overcome both the slowness and the mixed-state output of this approach.
AI.method: The unitary evolution of a 1D XY spin chain, with qubits coupled to its ends, is interspersed with measurements on the intermediate (intermediary) spins. Two measurement strategies are explored: (i) a measurement that post-selects the intermediary spins onto a ground state, and (ii) local measurements in the computational basis. The scheme is illustrated for qubits attached to the ends of the chain.
AI.result: Both measurement-assisted protocols (a) accelerate the establishment of entanglement via spin-chain dynamics and (b) produce a pure entangled state after a single use of the channel, which can be upgraded to a Bell state without the overhead of entanglement purification.
AI.conclusion: Measurement interspersed with spin-chain unitary dynamics offers a practical route to fast, single-shot generation of pure—and Bell—entanglement between distant qubits, circumventing the need for repeated channel uses and entanglement distillation.

title: Anomalous corrections to the inverse participation ratio in the localized phase on the Bethe lattice: insights from a solvable "toy" non-linear $σ$-model
comment: 40 pages, 17 figures. Companion paper to the Letter "Corrections to the IPR in the localized phase of the Anderson model on the Bethe lattice"
summary: In the localized phase of the Anderson model on the Bethe lattice, the inverse participation ratio (IPR) approaches its asymptotic value as the imaginary regulator $η\to 0$ with an anomalous power law, $I_2(η) - I_2^\infty \propto η^{2β-1}$, where $β\in (1/2,1)$ is the tail exponent of the local density of states distribution. We derive it analytically in a "toy" non-linear $σ$-model on the hyperbolic superplane, which shares the exotic criticality of the Bethe-lattice Anderson transition. Matching the bulk solution of its cavity equation to a boundary layer set by the symmetry-breaking field $H$ gives a correction $\propto H^{2β-1}$, controlled by the subdominant root $1-β$ of the linearized equation; at criticality it becomes $\propto 1/|\ln H|$. Under a few natural assumptions the same mechanism operates in the Anderson model, where the correction is a zero mode of the $η=0$ cavity recursion, as we confirm numerically, also for finite-size corrections. Through a spectral identity and an exact sum rule, the same exponent fixes exactly the decay $ω^{-μ}$, with $μ= 2(1-β)$, of the correlation function of two eigenstates at energy distance $ω$, including its amplitude, as we confirm by exact diagonalization, population dynamics on the infinite lattice, and analytically in the toy model. A counting of Mott resonances between distant localized eigenstates explains this physically; on finite graphs, finite-size corrections reflect a deficit of doubly-peaked eigenstates. Finally, we derive the finite-size scaling of the IPR in the variable $(2β-1)\ln N$, which describes both finite-$η$ and finite-$N$ data. It yields a Kosterlitz-type renormalization-group flow of the running fractal dimension: finite fractal dimensions of localized states at accessible sizes are a logarithmic finite-size effect.

AI.tldr: The anomalous power-law approach of the IPR to its asymptotic value in the localized phase of the Bethe-lattice Anderson model, $I_2(\eta)-I_2^\infty \propto \eta^{2\beta-1}$, is derived analytically in a toy non-linear $\sigma$-model and traced to the tail exponent $\beta$; the same exponent governs the eigenstate correlation decay $\omega^{-\mu}$ with $\mu=2(1-\beta)$ and a logarithmic finite-size scaling of the IPR.
AI.motivation: In the localized phase of the Anderson model on the Bethe lattice, the inverse participation ratio has long been known to converge anomalously slowly as the imaginary regulator $\eta\to0$, yet a controlled analytical understanding of the exponent and of its broader consequences (eigenstate correlations, finite-size effects) was missing. The paper aims to explain the microscopic origin of this anomalous scaling and to connect it to other observables.
AI.method: A "toy" non-linear $\sigma$-model on the hyperbolic superplane, sharing the exotic criticality of the Bethe-lattice Anderson transition, is solved by matching the bulk solution of its cavity equation to a boundary layer set by the symmetry-breaking field $H$. The resulting correction $\propto H^{2\beta-1}$ is controlled by the subdominant root $1-\beta$ of the linearized equation. A spectral identity and an exact sum rule are then used to relate the same exponent to eigenstate correlations; results are checked by exact diagonalization, population dynamics on the infinite lattice, and analytically in the toy model. Mott resonance counting provides a physical interpretation.
AI.result: The IPR corrections scale as $\eta^{2\beta-1}$, becoming $\propto 1/|\ln H|$ at criticality; the same mechanism acts in the Anderson model as a zero mode of the $\eta=0$ cavity recursion, confirmed numerically including finite-size corrections. The eigenstate correlation function at energy distance $\omega$ decays as $\omega^{-\mu}$ with $\mu=2(1-\beta)$, including its amplitude, verified by exact diagonalization and population dynamics. Finite-size scaling of the IPR is obtained in the variable $(2\beta-1)\ln N$, describing both finite-$\eta$ and finite-$N$ data.
AI.conclusion: The anomalous IPR scaling is a universal consequence of the subdominant cavity mode and is tied to eigenstate correlations via a spectral identity/sum rule, with Mott resonances giving the physical picture. Finite-size corrections reflect a deficit of doubly-peaked eigenstates, and the resulting Kosterlitz-type RG flow of the running fractal dimension implies that finite fractal dimensions observed at accessible sizes are a logarithmic finite-size effect.

title: Tailored Magic States for Algorithmic Primitives
summary: Algorithmic primitives such as adders, multipliers, and Boolean logic typically contain clusters of multi-qubit non-Clifford gates, whose decomposition into $T$ and $CCZ$ gates adds scheduling and spacetime overhead in fault-tolerant quantum computers. Synthillation addresses this difficulty for diagonal circuits at the third level of the Clifford hierarchy by jointly synthesizing and distilling their non-Clifford content. In this work, we develop a complementary, code-theoretic approach to synthillation. We introduce CSS-T-Product (CSS-TP) codes, whose transversal single-qubit phase gates implement multi-qubit logical diagonal gates, and give analytical rules that predict these logical gates from tensor-network operations. Using quantum LEGO, we generate code families with logical actions at the third and fourth levels of the Clifford hierarchy. We classify the resulting resource states as canonical (such as $T$ or $CCZ$), tensor products of canonical states, or irreducible, i.e., not reducible to a product of non-Clifford gates via Clifford operations and logical basis changes. Conversion into Encode-$T$-Decode factories built from these codes recover known synthillation resources and prepare magic states at higher levels of the Clifford hierarchy; we analyze them with a surface-code-based model for several algorithmic primitives. We demonstrate that tailored magic factories give significant latency improvements at similar or smaller occupied spacetime volume: at code distance $21$ with one factory per resource family, they reduce the latency of a $GF(2^{8})$ multiplier and a shared-addend carry-lookahead adder by up to $48\%$ and $38\%$, respectively, and the smallest tailored factory also lowers the occupied spacetime volume. CSS-TP codes thus connect code construction to resource factories for specific algorithmic primitives.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces CSS-T-Product (CSS-TP) codes, a code-theoretic framework for synthillation, whose transversal single-qubit phase gates realize multi-qubit logical diagonal gates, and uses them to build tailored magic-state factories that reduce latency and spacetime volume for arithmetic primitives in fault-tolerant quantum computing.
AI.motivation: Algorithmic primitives (adders, multipliers, Boolean logic) contain clusters of multi-qubit non-Clifford gates whose decomposition into T and CCZ gates incurs scheduling and spacetime overhead in fault-tolerant quantum computers. Synthillation mitigates this for diagonal circuits only at the third level of the Clifford hierarchy and lacks a general code-theoretic foundation; the authors seek a complementary code-based approach that can also produce higher-level resources.
AI.method: They define CSS-TP codes in which transversal single-qubit phase gates implement multi-qubit logical diagonal gates, and derive analytical rules predicting these logical gates from tensor-network operations. Using quantum LEGO, they generate code families with logical actions at the third and fourth levels of the Clifford hierarchy, and classify the resulting resource states as canonical (T, CCZ), tensor products of canonical states, or irreducible. These codes are converted into Encode-T-Decode factories and evaluated under a surface-code-based model for several algorithmic primitives.
AI.result: The construction recovers known synthillation resources and prepares magic states at higher Clifford-hierarchy levels. Under a surface-code model at code distance 21 with one factory per resource family, tailored factories reduce the latency of a GF(2^8) multiplier and a shared-addend carry-lookahead adder by up to 48% and 38%, respectively, at similar or smaller occupied spacetime volume; the smallest tailored factory also reduces occupied spacetime volume.
AI.conclusion: CSS-TP codes bridge code construction and resource factories for specific algorithmic primitives, providing a systematic, code-theoretic route to synthillation and to tailored magic-state production with improved latency and spacetime efficiency.

title: Statistical mechanics of linear classification on hierarchical tree data
summary: Deep networks owe much of their success to their ability to exploit the structure in data, from the grammar of language to the multi-scale organization of images. Yet, many statistical mechanics approaches to structured data rely on Gaussian equivalence, whose assumptions can fail when a few latent variables influence all input coordinates. In this work, we take a step beyond this setting with a simple setup, in which a linear classifier is trained to infer the root of the classical broadcast process on a tree from its $N$ leaves. Despite this simplicity, the data already display non-Gaussian statistics along the direction carrying the label, as well as strong finite-size effects. By retaining the exact law along this direction and approximating the transverse fluctuations as Gaussian, we obtain a finite-depth replica theory that accurately describes the measured learning curves. At large depth and sufficiently weak regularization, we uncover a double descent whose two stages are separated in scale. In a range of broadcast noise below the reconstruction threshold, the first descent occurs at a number of samples scaling as $N^ω$, with $0<ω<1$ set by the data statistics, whereas the overfitting peak occurs at order $N$ samples. Beyond linear classifiers, this setup could serve as a controlled starting point to study deeper architectures and generative models on hierarchical data.

AI.tldr: The authors analyze learning curves for a linear classifier inferring the root label of a broadcast process on a tree from its N leaves, developing a finite-depth replica theory that treats the label-carrying direction exactly and transverse fluctuations as Gaussian. This reveals a two-stage double descent, with the first descent at N^ω samples (0<ω<1) and the overfitting peak at O(N) samples.
AI.motivation: Much statistical-mechanics work on structured data relies on Gaussian equivalence, whose assumptions break down when a few latent variables influence all input coordinates—exactly the regime of hierarchical/broadcast data. The authors seek a tractable, controlled setting that moves beyond Gaussian-equivalent statistics while remaining analytically solvable.
AI.method: A minimal setup: a linear classifier trained to infer the root of the classical broadcast process on a tree from its N leaves. The data exhibit non-Gaussian statistics along the label-carrying direction plus strong finite-size effects. The authors keep the exact law along that direction and approximate transverse fluctuations as Gaussian, yielding a finite-depth replica theory.
AI.result: The finite-depth replica theory accurately reproduces measured learning curves. At large depth and weak regularization, a double descent emerges whose two stages are separated in scale: below the reconstruction threshold (in broadcast noise), the first descent occurs at a sample count scaling as N^ω with 0<ω<1 determined by data statistics, while the overfitting peak occurs at O(N) samples.
AI.conclusion: The work provides a controlled starting point beyond Gaussian equivalence for structured, hierarchical data, and could be extended to study deeper architectures and generative models.

title: Incompressible quantum information
summary: For a small classical system correlated with a large one, it is always possible to compress the large system down to a size only dependent on the size of the smaller one, while preserving all correlations up to a given controllable error. Here, we show that such a statement does not hold at all when the large system is quantum mechanical. More precisely, we show that there are bipartite states such that any compression of the large system, by a non-trivial relative factor, will necessarily lead to the destruction of a significant amount of correlation, measured in mutual information. Our results therefore identify a limitation of information-bottleneck approaches to quantum machine learning, showing that a small system specifying the relevant features contained in a large quantum data set does not guarantee a compact encoding of the latter that preserves the relevant correlations.

AI.tldr: Unlike classical systems, a large quantum system cannot in general be compressed to a size depending only on the correlated small system while preserving correlations; any non-trivial compression of the large system will destroy a significant amount of mutual-information correlation.
AI.motivation: The classical intuition that a large system correlated with a small one can be compressed to a dimension set by the small system (preserving all correlations up to controllable error) is widely assumed, and underpins information-bottleneck approaches to (quantum) machine learning. The authors test whether this compression statement survives in the quantum setting.
AI.method: Construct bipartite quantum states and analyze the effect of compressing the large subsystem by a non-trivial relative factor, bounding the resulting loss of correlation quantified by mutual information.
AI.result: There exist bipartite states for which any compression of the large system by a non-trivial relative factor necessarily destroys a significant amount of mutual-information correlation—showing the classical compression statement fails completely for quantum systems.
AI.conclusion: The results establish a fundamental limitation of information-bottleneck approaches to quantum machine learning: a small system specifying the relevant features of a large quantum data set does not guarantee a compact encoding that preserves the relevant correlations.

title: Online Scheduling for Entanglement Distillation: Learning When to Wait
summary: Entanglement distillation probabilistically increases the fidelity of entangled pairs at the cost of reducing their number. The outcome of each distillation operation takes time to communicate, during which the entangled pairs decohere while idle in their memories. This raises a dilemma: wait for the outcome before proceeding, or continue optimistically at the risk of needlessly consuming further pairs. We study online distillation scheduling, in which distillation trees are constructed dynamically to maximize the throughput of pairs that meet a required fidelity. A policy decides which pairs to distill together and, for each operation, whether to wait for its outcome. We derive an upper bound on the throughput of every scheduling policy and, by formulating the problem as a Markov decision process, train, with reinforcement learning, a policy that applies to any number of memories. Compared with two baselines that always or never wait, the learned policy delivers as many pairs of the required fidelity as the better one when one of these two extremes is the best choice, and more otherwise.

AI.tldr: The paper studies online scheduling of entanglement distillation, formulating it as an MDP and training a reinforcement-learning policy that decides which pairs to distill together and whether to wait for each operation's outcome, provably bounded and beating wait/never-wait baselines.
AI.motivation: Entanglement distillation consumes pairs to raise fidelity, and each operation's outcome takes time to communicate, during which idle pairs decohere in memory. This creates a dilemma: wait for the outcome before continuing, or proceed optimistically at the risk of wasting further pairs. A principled online policy is needed to maximize the throughput of pairs meeting a required fidelity.
AI.method: The problem is framed as online distillation scheduling with dynamically constructed distillation trees. A policy chooses which pairs to distill together and, per operation, whether to wait for its outcome. The authors first derive an upper bound on achievable throughput, then formulate the scheduling problem as a Markov decision process and train a reinforcement-learning policy that generalizes to any number of memories.
AI.result: The derived bound upper-limits the throughput of every scheduling policy. Empirically, against two baselines that always or never wait, the learned policy matches the better baseline whenever one of these extremes is optimal and exceeds both otherwise, yielding more pairs of the required fidelity.
AI.conclusion: Adaptive, learned waiting decisions outperform fixed always-wait or never-wait strategies, showing that RL-based online scheduling is an effective and scalable approach to entanglement distillation under decoherence.

title: Verification and Evaluation of A Comprehensive Quantum Simulation Compiler
summary: Hamiltonian simulation is a central application of quantum computing, yet most existing compilers offer no machine-checked guarantee that the circuits they produce approximate the intended evolution. The previous QBlue compiler verifies a Hamiltonian simulation compiler containing only Trotter-based algorithms. It takes a Hamiltonian written over Pauli strings, a simulation time, and an error bound, and produces a circuit or analog schedule that is proven, in the Rocq proof assistant, to approximate the ideal time evolution within that bound and proves a single end-to-end error bound that composes the errors of the individual stages; the compiler uses it to select, by resource estimation, the cheapest algorithm that meets the user's bound. This paper advances the verification efforts with two further steps. First, we extend QBlue to $\textsf{QBlue}_{\texttt{BE}}$ by verifying another important compilation method for Hamiltonian simulation: block-encoding-based (BE-based) algorithms. Second, we empirically evaluate 279 Hamiltonian simulation programs against the state-of-the-art BE-based compiler, PennyLane. For many programs, our compiler shows a $94\%$ gate reduction compared to PennyLane. Additionally, we also discover issues and bugs in PennyLane. We also compare Trotter- and BE-based algorithms, providing a practical comparison for the long-standing debate over which algorithms perform better. Our results surprisingly show that Trotter-based algorithms may gain a practical advantage, even though BE algorithms have a theoretical advantage.

AI.tldr: The paper extends the verified QBlue compiler with block-encoding-based Hamiltonian simulation, producing Rocq-proven circuits with composed error bounds, and empirically shows up to 94% gate reduction versus PennyLane while finding bugs there and finding Trotter methods often practically superior.
AI.motivation: Most Hamiltonian simulation compilers lack machine-checked guarantees that their output circuits approximate the intended evolution. QBlue previously verified only Trotter-based algorithms; block-encoding-based methods, an important theoretical class, remained unverified, and the practical performance of Trotter versus BE algorithms was unresolved.
AI.method: Extend QBlue to QBlue_BE by formally verifying block-encoding-based Hamiltonian simulation algorithms in Rocq, preserving the end-to-end error bound composition and resource-estimation-based algorithm selection. Then evaluate 279 Hamiltonian simulation programs against the state-of-the-art BE-based compiler PennyLane, and compare Trotter- and BE-based algorithms.
AI.result: For many programs the verified compiler achieves a 94% gate reduction over PennyLane; issues and bugs are identified in PennyLane. Comparative results show Trotter-based algorithms can hold a practical advantage despite the theoretical advantage of BE algorithms.
AI.conclusion: Machine-checked verification can be extended to BE-based Hamiltonian simulation, yielding substantial practical resource savings and revealing both bugs in an existing tool and a gap between theoretical and practical performance of algorithm classes.

title: Froq: Safe Speculative Execution on Live Quantum States for FTQC
summary: Reducing execution time is critical to fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC) as longer executions expose logical qubits to more opportunities for failure. However, quantum processors could frequently stall due to slow classical error-correction decoders. Recent speculative decoding accelerates this process, but its speculation remains on the classical side, leaving quantum operations waiting for confirmed decoding results. Extending speculative execution to the quantum side is fundamentally challenging. Unlike classical processor states, quantum states cannot be arbitrarily copied or checkpointed for rollback, making recovery from mispredictions difficult. In this work, we propose Froq to enable safe speculative execution on live quantum states. Froq uses compiler-assisted recovery contracts to track how mispredictions propagate through quantum operations. It further employs a resource-aware runtime mechanism to reserve recovery workspace and dynamically balance the benefits of speculative execution against the expected costs of recovery. We evaluate Froq on eight FTQC programs across 88 configurations, building on an existing speculative window decoder. Froq reduces quantum-side time by 9.81% across all 88 configurations. The reduction reaches 18.34% across the 45 configurations allowing concurrent predictions, and peaks at 31.1% at code distance d=21, under limited resources.

AI.tldr: Froq enables safe speculative execution on live quantum states to reduce quantum-side execution time in fault-tolerant quantum computing, using compiler-assisted recovery contracts and a resource-aware runtime.
AI.motivation: Reducing execution time is critical to fault-tolerant quantum computing (FTQC), since longer executions expose logical qubits to more chances of failure. Quantum processors can stall due to slow classical error-correction decoders; recent speculative decoding accelerates decoding but speculation remains classical-side, leaving quantum operations waiting for confirmed decoding results. Extending speculation to the quantum side is hard because quantum states cannot be arbitrarily copied or checkpointed for rollback, complicating recovery from mispredictions.
AI.method: The authors propose Froq, which enables safe speculative execution on live quantum states. It uses compiler-assisted recovery contracts to track how mispredictions propagate through quantum operations, and employs a resource-aware runtime mechanism that reserves recovery workspace and dynamically balances the benefits of speculative execution against the expected costs of recovery.
AI.result: Froq is evaluated on eight FTQC programs across 88 configurations, building on an existing speculative window decoder. It reduces quantum-side time by 9.81% across all 88 configurations. The reduction reaches 18.34% across the 45 configurations allowing concurrent predictions, and peaks at 31.1% at code distance d=21 under limited resources.
AI.conclusion: Froq demonstrates that speculative execution can be safely extended to the quantum side, mitigating decoders-induced stalls and reducing FTQC quantum-side execution time, with particularly strong gains when concurrent predictions are possible and at larger code distances under limited resources.

title: Causal Consistency and Cost of Quantum Control
summary: An unknown quantum state can supply the information needed to control a computation, but how much quantum data must be consumed to perform a prescribed action? We connect this resource question to causal consistency within the quantum state space. No-signaling requires identical observable predictions for remotely chosen ensemble preparations of the same complete input; quantum distinguishability then converts this requirement into finite-copy bounds. For amplitude amplification, we identify an exact low-copy obstruction and establish a dimension-independent, optimal quadratic dependence of the copy cost on angular gain at fixed accuracy, uniformly over arbitrary pure inputs. A coherent protocol attains this scaling without reconstructing a classical state description. Prior knowledge of a real two-level family additionally permits exponentially decreasing error with the copy budget at fixed gain. These results separate the resources needed to perform a specified quantum operation from those needed for universal state reconstruction. The central connection is operational: physical consistency restricts which distinctions a controller can expose, and the information carried by its complete input determines the cost of doing so. This links a causal requirement to quantitative limits on converting quantum data into computational control.

AI.tldr: Quantum-state-copy resources needed for amplitude amplification are shown to be governed by no-signaling/causal consistency: an exact low-copy obstruction is identified, and an optimal, dimension-independent quadratic copy cost in angular gain (at fixed accuracy, uniformly over pure inputs) is attained by a coherent protocol without classical state reconstruction, while prior knowledge of a real two-level family yields exponentially decreasing error with copy budget.
AI.motivation: An unknown quantum state can provide the information required to control a computation, but how many copies of the quantum data must be consumed to implement a prescribed operation is unclear. The paper asks this resource question and relates it to causal consistency (no-signaling) inside quantum state space, aiming to separate the resources needed for a specified quantum operation from those needed for universal state reconstruction.
AI.method: The authors exploit no-signaling: remotely chosen ensemble preparations of the same complete input must yield identical observable predictions, and quantum distinguishability turns this into finite-copy bounds. They apply this framework to amplitude amplification, derive an exact low-copy obstruction via distinguishability arguments, and construct a coherent protocol achieving the optimal copy scaling without reconstructing a classical state description.
AI.result: For amplitude amplification, an exact low-copy obstruction is identified, and an optimal quadratic dependence of copy cost on angular gain at fixed accuracy is established, uniformly over arbitrary pure inputs and independently of dimension. A coherent protocol attains this scaling without classical state tomography. With prior knowledge of a real two-level family, error decreases exponentially with the copy budget at fixed gain.
AI.conclusion: Resources required to perform a specified quantum operation are distinct from those required for universal state reconstruction. The central link is operational: physical consistency constrains which distinctions a controller can expose, and the information in the complete input fixes the cost of doing so—connecting a causal requirement to quantitative limits on converting quantum data into computational control.

title: Coherent Control of Single-Photon Emission in Broadband Plasmonic Resonators
summary: Encoding phase information with quantum emitters in metallic optical nanocavities is challenging due to ultrafast relaxation induced by the broadband nature of the plasmonic near field. Using macroscopic quantum electrodynamics theory, we demonstrate that an individual emitter strongly coupled to a plasmonic nanocavity field that is driven by a pulsed laser with frequency comb spectrum undergoes spontaneous emission of well-resolved one-photon pulses whose amplitude scales quadratically with the number of frequency comb components due to coherent accumulation, and ultrashort non-exponential temporal profiles with duration set by the light-matter coupling strength. Conditions are discussed for exponentially suppressing the probability of two or more emission events within the lifetime of the coupled emitter-nanocavity system. The spectral signatures of the optimal one-photon wavepackets are discussed. This work paves the way for the development of ultrafast laser-triggered single-photon emitters using atoms and molecules in optical nanocavities.

AI.tldr: An emitter strongly coupled to a plasmonic nanocavity driven by a frequency-comb pulse emits well-resolved ultrafast single-photon wavepackets, with amplitude scaling quadratically with comb-component number due to coherent accumulation.
AI.motivation: Encoding phase information with quantum emitters in metallic optical nanocavities is difficult because the broadband plasmonic near field causes ultrafast relaxation. The authors aim to enable ultrafast laser-triggered single-photon emission from atoms/molecules in optical nanocavities.
AI.method: Macroscopic quantum electrodynamics (QED) theory is used to model an individual emitter strongly coupled to a plasmonic nanocavity field driven by a pulsed laser with a frequency-comb spectrum.
AI.result: The emitter undergoes spontaneous emission of well-resolved one-photon pulses whose amplitude scales quadratically with the number of frequency-comb components (coherent accumulation), with ultrashort non-exponential temporal profiles set by the light-matter coupling strength. Conditions for exponentially suppressing multi-photon (two or more) emission events over the coupled system lifetime are discussed, along with spectral signatures of optimal one-photon wavepackets.
AI.conclusion: Frequency-comb-driven strong coupling in plasmonic nanocavities offers a route to ultrafast laser-triggered single-photon emitters using atoms and molecules.

title: photon number correlations in harmonics driven with classical and quantum light
comment: 13 pages (8 main, 5 supplemental), 8 figures (5 main, 3 supplemental), Submitted to Optics Express
summary: Recent reports of nonclassical intensity correlations in harmonic generation raised questions about whether strong harmonic correlations necessarily imply genuinely quantum behaviour. Here, we compare the low-photon-number perturbative harmonic generation driven by classical and bright squeezed vacuum sources. The latter generates strong auto- and cross-correlations in the harmonic spectrum. Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and heralding measurements show that the cross-correlations are fully classical and can be explained by the common fluctuations from the driving field. A visible scaling of the measured correlation function with mean harmonic flux is observed, which is well-explained by a click detector-response model.

AI.tldr: Strong intensity correlations in harmonic generation are shown to be classical: the cross-correlations arise from common fluctuations in the driving bright squeezed vacuum, not from genuinely quantum effects.
AI.motivation: Recent reports of nonclassical intensity correlations in harmonic generation raised the question of whether strong harmonic correlations necessarily imply genuinely quantum behaviour, motivating a direct comparison between classical and bright squeezed vacuum driving at low photon numbers.
AI.method: The authors compare low-photon-number perturbative harmonic generation driven by classical versus bright squeezed vacuum sources, measuring auto- and cross-correlations in the harmonic spectrum and testing them against the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality together with heralding measurements.
AI.result: Bright squeezed vacuum driving produces strong auto- and cross-correlations in the harmonic spectrum, but the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality and heralding measurements reveal the cross-correlations to be fully classical, attributable to common fluctuations of the driving field. A visible scaling of the measured correlation function with mean harmonic flux is observed and is well described by a click detector-response model.
AI.conclusion: Strong harmonic intensity correlations do not by themselves certify nonclassicality; they can be fully explained by classical driving-field fluctuations, and detector response must be accounted for when interpreting such correlation measurements.

title: Subquantum Pilot-Wave System Theory: Structural and Amplitude Nonequilibrium under Source Fields
summary: A source in the Schrodinger equation changes the norm of the guiding wave, apparently conflicting with the conservation of probability. In source-extended de Broglie-Bohm dynamics the conflict disappears: probability is carried by the particle ensemble, while the wavefunction guides its motion. The difficulty is then different. What does quantum equilibrium mean when the particle distribution remains normalized but the guiding density does not? We show that the departure has two independent components: a structural one, measured by the Kullback--Leibler divergence between the particle distribution and the normalized guiding density, and an amplitude one, measured by the Born weight. The Born rule holds precisely when both are equilibrated. Their evolution is governed by the complex source-to-wavefunction ratio; scale covariance further distinguishes an independently prescribed source, against which the amplitude of the wave matters, from state-dependent generators for which rescaling remains a symmetry. We develop a source-aware analytical--computational method, combining exact or semi-analytical guiding fields with Bohmian trajectory transport, ensemble quadrature and independent numerical checks. Free-space impulses expose the limits of global diagnostics and an exact jump rule; a driven ring has constant Born weight but either periodic or secular structural departure; oscillators show both source-generated structural change and amplitude-only evolution, including a finite-horizon weak-drive plateau far below its frozen-particle value; and a coupled two-body model exhibits nonlocal guidance and evolving particle entanglement. The source-free, initially equilibrated sector recovers standard quantum mechanics.

AI.tldr: Source terms in the Schrödinger equation break the norm of the guiding wave, so the paper recasts quantum equilibrium in source-extended de Broglie–Bohm dynamics as a two-component departure (structural + amplitude) and builds a source-aware analytical-computational framework to track it.
AI.motivation: A source in the Schrödinger equation changes the guiding-wave norm, which seems to conflict with probability conservation; in source-extended Bohmian dynamics probability is carried by the particle ensemble rather than the wave, but this raises a new question: what quantum equilibrium means when the particle distribution stays normalized while the guiding density does not.
AI.method: Decompose the departure from equilibrium into a structural component (Kullback–Leibler divergence between particle distribution and normalized guiding density) and an amplitude component (Born weight); analyze their evolution via the complex source-to-wavefunction ratio and scale covariance (distinguishing independently prescribed sources from state-dependent generators); develop a source-aware analytical–computational method combining exact/semi-analytical guiding fields, Bohmian trajectory transport, ensemble quadrature, and independent numerical checks.
AI.result: Born rule holds only when both components are equilibrated. Free-space impulses reveal limits of global diagnostics and yield an exact jump rule; a driven ring shows constant Born weight with either periodic or secular structural departure; oscillators exhibit both source-generated structural change and amplitude-only evolution, including a finite-horizon weak-drive plateau far below the frozen-particle value; a coupled two-body model shows nonlocal guidance and evolving particle entanglement. The source-free, initially equilibrated sector recovers standard quantum mechanics.
AI.conclusion: Quantum equilibrium under sources is a two-condition (structural and amplitude) property, and source-extended Bohmian dynamics consistently accommodates non-norm-preserving guiding waves while reducing to standard quantum mechanics in the source-free, equilibrated limit.

title: Quantum nonclassicality as a marginal problem
summary: Classical explanations of quantum statistics---local, noncontextual, or causal---fail for one and the same reason: the probability distributions observed in different contexts are not the marginals of a single joint distribution. Every single context admits a classical model. This is Boole's problem of the "conditions of possible experience." Garg and Mermin treated it as a linear problem and showed, via Farkas's lemma, that its solvability is equivalent to a finite list of Bell-type inequalities, one for each extreme ray of a convex polyhedral cone; Pitowsky gave it the form of correlation polytopes. We sketch this common structure and discuss two examples: Aerts's elastic-band model, which reproduces the quantum cosine in one context but obeys the classical bound when contexts are combined; and nonclassicality in causal data fusion, where the contexts are supplied by interventions on a causal structure.

AI.tldr: Classical explanations of quantum statistics (local, noncontextual, causal) all fail for the same reason: context-indexed probability distributions are not marginals of one joint distribution. This is Boole's "conditions of possible experience," a linear feasibility problem solvable iff Bell-type inequalities for every extreme ray of a polyhedral cone (Farkas; Garg–Mermin; Pitowsky's correlation polytopes) hold. Two illustrations: Aerts's elastic-band model and nonclassicality in causal data fusion.
AI.motivation: To unify disparate classicality notions (locality, noncontextuality, causality) under one formal criterion, and to connect quantum-foundational arguments with a broader data-analysis setting (causal data fusion), showing they share a single geometric/linear-algebraic obstruction rather than distinct physical mechanisms.
AI.method: Formulate context-dependent distributions as a question of existence of a single joint distribution having them as marginals (Boole's problem). Cast this as a linear feasibility problem, apply Farkas's lemma to obtain an equivalent finite list of Bell-type inequalities indexed by extreme rays of a convex polyhedral cone, and use the correlation-polytope framing. Illustrate via (i) Aerts's elastic-band model and (ii) causal data fusion where "contexts" arise from interventions on a causal structure.
AI.result: All three classical explanations fail by the identical criterion (no common joint distribution / marginal-consistency violation). Each individual context is classically modelable; inconsistency emerges only upon combining contexts. Aerts's model reproduces the quantum cosine within one context yet satisfies the classical bound when contexts are combined; the causal-data-fusion case exhibits nonclassicality when intervention-supplied contexts are jointly analyzed.
AI.conclusion: Quantum statistical nonclassicality across locality, contextuality, and causality is one phenomenon: failure of marginal-consistency/Boole's conditions of possible experience, characterized by Bell-type inequalities from the polyhedral cone's extreme rays. This reframes foundational debates as a general marginal problem with applications beyond physics, e.g., causal data fusion.

title: Revealing the Hidden Symmetry of the Asymmetric Quantum Rabi Model
summary: A longitudinal bias breaks ordinary parity in the asymmetric quantum Rabi model, yet exact crossings reappear when the bias equals an integer multiple $m$ of the oscillator energy spacing. We trace the hidden symmetry to exchange between equal-energy partners $m$ rungs apart on two displaced oscillator ladders. Tunneling to other rungs makes this exchange vary in time. We construct the exact symmetry operator by adding spin and oscillator coherences that cancel this variation. At nonzero coupling and tunneling, the resulting charge has no zero modes, and its sign divides the full Hilbert space into two generalized-parity sectors that cannot mix. Spin-resolved mirror interference probes coherence between the two opposite-parity states at a crossing. Its small-displacement exponent gives $m$, and its leading coefficient, together with the charge magnitude, predicts the mixing induced by a slight change in bias.

AI.tldr: A longitudinal bias breaks parity in the asymmetric quantum Rabi model, but exact crossings recur when the bias equals an integer multiple m of the oscillator spacing. The hidden symmetry is an unbroken, coherence-corrected conserved charge with no zero modes; its sign defines two non-mixing generalized-parity sectors, and spin-resolved mirror interference extracts m and predicts bias-induced mixing.
AI.motivation: Ordinary parity is broken by a longitudinal bias in the asymmetric quantum Rabi model, yet exact (diabatic) crossings unexpectedly reappear at commensurate bias values. The paper seeks the hidden symmetry responsible and a way to characterize and exploit it spectroscopically.
AI.method: Trace the hidden symmetry to an exchange between equal-energy partners m rungs apart on two displaced oscillator ladders; treat inter-rung tunneling as a time-varying exchange; construct the exact symmetry operator by adding spin and oscillator coherences that cancel this variation; analyze its charge spectrum; and propose spin-resolved mirror interference to probe coherence between opposite-parity states at a crossing.
AI.result: At nonzero coupling and tunneling the conserved charge has no zero modes, and its sign partitions the full Hilbert space into two generalized-parity sectors that cannot mix. The spin-resolved interference signal's small-displacement exponent yields m, and its leading coefficient together with the charge magnitude predicts the mixing induced by a slight change in bias.
AI.conclusion: The commensurate crossings are protected by an exact, coherence-dressed generalized parity rather than ordinary parity, providing a robust label for the asymmetric quantum Rabi model and a spectroscopic protocol to read m and quantify residual mixing.

title: Phase-dependent atomicity and PPT edge states for cyclic-sign covariant qutrit maps
summary: Decomposable positive maps cannot detect entangled states with positive partial transpose (PPT). We obtain a necessary and sufficient criterion for decomposability in the entire seven-real-parameter class of Hermiticity-preserving cyclic-sign covariant maps on $M_3$. The criterion reduces to a one-variable inequality and, for positive maps in this class, characterizes indecomposability exactly. We apply it to a phase-dependent family obtained by adding a completely positive map to the Choi map. Every map in this family is positive, and we find the exact phase-dependent threshold for indecomposability and atomicity. At three phase values, the maps remain indecomposable for every finite deformation strength. Each indecomposable map gives an indecomposable entanglement witness through its Choi matrix. We construct PPT edge states of birank $(5,5)$ detected by these witnesses throughout the indecomposable region.

AI.tldr: The authors derive a necessary and sufficient decomposability criterion for the full seven-real-parameter class of Hermiticity-preserving cyclic-sign covariant maps on M3, reducing it to a single-variable inequality, and apply it to a phase-dependent family built from the Choi map to obtain exact phase-dependent thresholds for indecomposability and atomicity.
AI.motivation: Decomposable positive maps cannot detect PPT entangled states, so identifying indecomposable maps is essential for entanglement detection. The broader seven-parameter covariant class on M3 lacked an exact decomposability criterion, leaving the entanglement-detection power of most maps in this class uncharacterized.
AI.method: The analysis covers the entire seven-real-parameter class of Hermiticity-preserving cyclic-sign covariant maps on M3. A necessary and sufficient decomposability criterion is derived and reduced to a one-variable inequality, giving an exact characterization of indecomposability for positive maps in the class. The criterion is then applied to a phase-dependent family formed by adding a completely positive map to the Choi map, determining thresholds for indecomposability and atomicity, and the resulting Choi matrices are used as entanglement witnesses to construct PPT edge states.
AI.result: The criterion exactly characterizes indecomposability for positive maps in the class. Every map in the phase-dependent family is positive, and exact phase-dependent thresholds for indecomposability and atomicity are obtained. At three phase values the maps remain indecomposable for every finite deformation strength. Each indecomposable map yields an indecomposable entanglement witness via its Choi matrix, and PPT edge states of birank (5,5) detected by these witnesses are constructed throughout the indecomposable region.
AI.conclusion: Decomposability in the seven-parameter cyclic-sign covariant class on M3 admits an exact one-variable criterion, enabling precise mapping of indecomposable and atomic regions. The construction provides explicit indecomposable witnesses and PPT edge states of birank (5,5) across the indecomposable region, with certain phase values yielding robustness against any finite deformation.

title: Many-Body Flux Selection in Chiral Quantum Batteries
summary: We study an interacting quantum-battery chain in which a synthetic flux controls interference between hopping paths. Keeping the internal battery Hamiltonian fixed, we seek the flux that leaves the most extractable work. Even a Gaussian reconstruction supplied with exact one-body information can rank competing flux settings incorrectly. A reduced many-body model that retains correlations within a few battery-occupation sectors recovers the correct ranking and selects nearly optimal fluxes across the finite systems and parameter ranges studied. Strikingly, the model can make an accurate control choice even when it excludes configurations carrying substantial probability in the exact state. Thus, choosing a nearly optimal charging flux can require much less information than reconstructing the full many-body state.

AI.tldr: A flux-tuned interacting quantum-battery chain is optimized by a reduced many-body model that retains correlations within a few battery-occupation sectors, which recovers the correct ranking of flux settings and nearly optimal work even when a Gaussian reconstruction with exact one-body data fails.
AI.motivation: Synthetic-flux-controlled interference between hopping paths offers a handle on extractable work in an interacting quantum battery, but the authors ask how much many-body information is actually required to select the flux that maximizes ergotropy. Standard reconstructions may misrank candidate fluxes.
AI.method: The internal battery Hamiltonian is held fixed while the synthetic flux is scanned. Benchmarks compare exact-state results with (i) a Gaussian (one-body) reconstruction fed exact one-body information and (ii) a reduced many-body model that keeps correlations only within a few battery-occupation sectors, tested across finite systems and parameter ranges.
AI.result: The Gaussian reconstruction can rank competing flux settings incorrectly despite exact one-body input. The sector-truncated many-body model restores the correct ranking and selects nearly optimal fluxes; notably, it succeeds even when it discards configurations that carry substantial probability in the exact state.
AI.conclusion: Choosing a nearly optimal charging flux requires far less information than full many-body-state reconstruction: retaining correlations in a few occupation sectors suffices for accurate control decisions, decoupling control-relevant information from global state fidelity.

title: Sharp Purity Based Entropy Bounds and Machine Learning Assisted Entropy Estimation
summary: Purity quantifies quantum-state mixedness, motivating the study of its role in controlling entropy variations. A sharp purity-based continuity bound is established for the von Neumann entropy of qubit states. The bound is attainable for every admissible purity difference and strictly improves the existing purity bound. In higher dimensions, an explicit sharp bound is derived within the family of pure states mixed with the maximally mixed state. Further continuity estimates are obtained for conditional entropy, quantum mutual information, quantum conditional mutual information, and squashed entanglement within specified bipartite and tripartite families. An application to machine learning assisted qubit entropy estimation illustrates how the sharp bound converts purity estimation errors into rigorous entropy error bounds.

AI.tldr: A sharp purity-based continuity bound for the von Neumann entropy of qubit states is established, attainable for every admissible purity difference and strictly improving existing bounds, with extensions to higher dimensions and several correlated entropic quantities, plus an application to machine-learning-assisted entropy estimation.
AI.motivation: Purity quantifies quantum-state mixedness and can control entropy variations, motivating a sharp, purity-based continuity relation for von Neumann entropy that tightens prior bounds and yields rigorous error control.
AI.method: Derive a sharp purity-based continuity bound for qubit von Neumann entropy; for higher dimensions, obtain an explicit sharp bound restricted to states that are mixtures of pure states with the maximally mixed state; extend continuity estimates to conditional entropy, quantum mutual information, quantum conditional mutual information, and squashed entanglement within specified bipartite and tripartite families.
AI.result: The qubit bound is attainable for every admissible purity difference and strictly improves the existing purity bound; the higher-dimensional bound is sharp within the considered family; further continuity estimates are obtained for the listed entropic quantities in the specified families.
AI.conclusion: The sharp purity-entropy continuity bounds provide tighter, attainable guarantees and, as illustrated by machine-learning-assisted qubit entropy estimation, convert purity estimation errors into rigorous entropy error bounds.

title: Quantum Metrology With Quantum Limit Cycles
summary: Beyond nonclassical states, emergent quantum phenomena offer new metrological resources. Quantum limit cycles, in particular, sustain long-lived oscillations that prolong coherent signal accumulation. However, quantum fluctuations may limit this advantage, leaving their metrological performance unclear. Here, we propose a quantum limit-cycle metrology protocol for collective spins by introducing nonlinear damping into the conventional collective-decay protocol. We develop a semiclassical phase-diffusion theory to characterize its metrological performance, in good agreement with numerical simulations. The limit-cycle protocol improves estimation precision and approaches Heisenberg scaling with system size. We further combine limit-cycle dynamics with spin squeezing, finding that squeezing improves short-time precision, but phase diffusion ultimately dominates, leaving the asymptotic scaling unchanged. Our results establish quantum limit cycles as a metrological resource and clarify the interplay between limit-cycle dynamics and squeezing in quantum sensing.

AI.tldr: The authors propose a quantum limit-cycle metrology protocol for collective spins by adding nonlinear damping to a collective-decay protocol, and develop a semiclassical phase-diffusion theory showing the protocol improves estimation precision and approaches Heisenberg scaling with system size, while squeezing only aids short-time precision.
AI.motivation: Emergent quantum phenomena such as quantum limit cycles offer potential metrological resources by sustaining long-lived oscillations that prolong coherent signal accumulation, but quantum fluctuations may limit this advantage, leaving the metrological performance of quantum limit cycles unclear.
AI.method: The authors introduce nonlinear damping into the conventional collective-decay protocol for collective spins to realize a quantum limit-cycle metrology protocol, and develop a semiclassical phase-diffusion theory to characterize its metrological performance, validated against numerical simulations. They also combine limit-cycle dynamics with spin squeezing.
AI.result: The semiclassical phase-diffusion theory agrees well with numerical simulations. The limit-cycle protocol improves estimation precision and approaches Heisenberg scaling with system size. Combining with spin squeezing improves short-time precision, but phase diffusion ultimately dominates, leaving the asymptotic scaling unchanged.
AI.conclusion: Quantum limit cycles are established as a metrological resource, and the interplay between limit-cycle dynamics and squeezing in quantum sensing is clarified, with phase diffusion identified as the asymptotic limiting factor.

title: Holevo-Bounded Total Information from Pair Distributions of Alternative Quantum Measurements
summary: The accessible information of a quantum ensemble can be strictly smaller than its Holevo information because a single-copy measurement may discard part of the label--system correlation. We ask whether information represented across two alternative measurement contexts can bridge this gap without assigning a joint distribution to their outcomes. Building on the relative-entropy-based projection method introduced by Harder et al., we define the directed posterior novelty of each record relative to the other, and an associated total-information quantity. For posterior-orthogonal records, this quantity equals the sum of the two record mutual informations. For finite-dimensional classical--quantum ensembles, we prove that optimizing this quantity over pairs of POVMs yields a value between the accessible and Holevo information. The upper bound follows by showing that the directed posterior novelty provides a lower bound on the infimum of the measured-relative-entropy recovery error. The uniform BB84 ensemble provides an example in which the quantity saturates the Holevo information while strictly exceeding the accessible information. Finally, we analytically establish the quantum validity of a redundancy-based information causality condition, resolving a question that has remained open since the condition was introduced.

AI.tldr: The paper studies whether information shared across two alternative measurement contexts can exceed the accessible information of a quantum ensemble. Building on a relative-entropy projection method, it defines directed posterior novelty and a total-information quantity that is bounded between accessible and Holevo information, saturates Holevo for BB84, and yields a redundancy-based information-causality condition.
AI.motivation: A single-copy measurement can discard part of the label–system correlation, so the accessible information may be strictly below the Holevo information. The authors ask whether information represented across two alternative measurement contexts can bridge this gap without requiring a joint distribution over their outcomes.
AI.method: Building on the relative-entropy-based projection method of Harder et al., the authors define the directed posterior novelty of each record relative to the other and an associated total-information quantity. They then optimize this quantity over pairs of POVMs for finite-dimensional classical–quantum ensembles, and bound it via the measured-relative-entropy recovery error.
AI.result: For posterior-orthogonal records the quantity equals the sum of the two record mutual informations. For finite-dimensional classical–quantum ensembles, the optimized quantity lies between the accessible and Holevo information; the upper bound follows from showing directed posterior novelty lower-bounds the infimum measured-relative-entropy recovery error. The uniform BB84 ensemble saturates the Holevo information while strictly exceeding the accessible information. The authors also analytically establish the quantum validity of a redundancy-based information-causality condition.
AI.conclusion: Cross-context information, quantified by the optimized directed posterior novelty, interpolates between accessible and Holevo information and can reach the Holevo value (BB84). This also settles an open question by proving the quantum validity of the redundancy-based information-causality condition.

title: Increasing Quantum LDPC Code Distance through Explicit Extensions
summary: We give an explicit construction of quantum low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes without searching for candidates at each size. A fixed pair partition (PP) and fixed integer parameters determine the parity-check matrices at a specified size. Using affine permutation matrices (APMs), we construct a $[[3072,772,32]]$ code with column weight 3 and check weight 8 in each of the X and Z parity-check matrices. A construction based on circulant permutation matrices (CPMs) gives $[[1270,260,\ge34]]$, with column weight 4 and check weight 10. We prove that the construction yields commuting checks and verify the resulting distances using exhaustive search and logical operators. For the main construction, we conjecture the existence of a finite structural distance upper bound and distance improvement toward that bound as the size increases.

AI.tldr: The paper gives an explicit, search-free construction of quantum LDPC codes using fixed pair partitions plus affine or circulant permutation matrices, yielding a [[3072,772,32]] code and a [[1270,260,≥34]] code.
AI.motivation: Existing quantum LDPC constructions typically require searching for candidate matrices at each code size, which is inefficient; the authors aim for a deterministic, size-parametrized construction.
AI.method: Fixed pair partition (PP) and fixed integer parameters define the parity-check matrices at a given size. Two instantiations are given: one using affine permutation matrices (APMs) with column weight 3 and check weight 8 in both X and Z checks, and one using circulant permutation matrices (CPMs) with column weight 4 and check weight 10. Commuting checks are proven, and distances are verified via exhaustive search and logical operators.
AI.result: An [[3072,772,32]] APM-based code (column weight 3, check weight 8 per X/Z matrix) and a [[1270,260,≥34]] CPM-based code (column weight 4, check weight 10) are constructed and their distances verified.
AI.conclusion: The PP-based construction yields valid commuting-check quantum LDPC codes without per-size search. The authors conjecture a finite structural distance upper bound for the main construction, with distance improving toward it as size grows.

title: The resource--invariant gap: a protected Floquet invariant need not protect Wigner negativity
comment: 32 pages, 6 figures, 3 tables. Supplemental Material: 49 pages, 5 figures, 28 tables
summary: Topological invariants constrain a driven Floquet generator, yet whether they protect a transient nonlinear bosonic resource remains open. We track boundary Wigner negativity of an even cat state in a chiral Floquet Su--Schrieffer--Heeger chain with boundary Kerr nonlinearity and structured loss. The quasienergy windings remain quantized at every chain length, yet the matched sector contrast flips sign when the chain grows under index-end shielding and is null within $3\times 10^{-5}$ under uniform loss at $t=T$ for $d\le 0.5$. Prepared and shielded on the physical dangling end, the contrast remains positive, modulated by local dimer return rather than set by the invariant. A three-site causal light cone and a boundary-Laplacian erosion law trace the flip to strong-bond bulk exposure: the sign is set by where the bulk-rate loss sits relative to the prepared site, not by chain length. We call this decoupling the resource--invariant gap.

AI.tldr: Topological quasienergy windings stay quantized in a chiral Floquet SSH chain, but the boundary Wigner negativity of an even cat state is not protected by them: its sign/contrast depends on where the bulk-rate loss sits relative to the prepared site, a "resource-invariant gap."
AI.motivation: It is open whether topological invariants of a driven (Floquet) bosonic generator actually protect a transient nonlinear bosonic resource such as boundary Wigner negativity.
AI.method: Track boundary Wigner negativity of an even cat state in a chiral Floquet Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain with boundary Kerr nonlinearity and structured loss; use index-end shielding, uniform loss, a three-site causal light cone, and a boundary-Laplacian erosion law to localize the effect.
AI.result: Quasienergy windings remain quantized at every chain length, yet matched-sector contrast flips sign with chain growth under index-end shielding and is null within 3e-5 under uniform loss at t=T for d<=0.5. When prepared and shielded on the physical dangling end, contrast stays positive, modulated by local dimer return rather than the invariant. The flip traces to strong-bond bulk exposure, i.e., bulk-rate loss position relative to the prepared site, not chain length.
AI.conclusion: Topological invariants do not guarantee protection of the boundary nonlinear bosonic resource; the resource-invariant gap is a decoupling where contrast sign is governed by loss placement relative to the prepared site, revealed by causal light-cone and boundary-Laplacian erosion analysis.

title: Long-time dynamics of open quantum systems: mathematical and physical aspects
summary: Quantum channels provide the mathematical framework for describing the evolution of open quantum systems, i.e., quantum systems interacting with an environment. This review focuses on the long-time or asymptotic dynamics of open quantum systems, a topic of growing interest due to its relevance for quantum information theory and noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices. We present a comprehensive analysis of homogeneous evolutions in both discrete and continuous time, treating the dynamics in full generality within the Schrödinger and Heisenberg pictures. By systematically studying the spectral properties of quantum channels, we present general structure theorems that characterize asymptotic behaviour, illustrated through several paradigmatic examples.
